Aeroswift

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
cutting edge laser research promises to give the South African aersopace industry lift-off

Unique Selling Point:
Researchers at CSIR, in partnership with aerospace company Aerosud and funded by the Department of Science and Technology, have developed what they say is the biggest 3D printer in the world. They are using it to print complex, specialised parts for aircraft - and our team will watch as they are flight-tested in the first-ever fully South African-designed and made aircraft, AHRLAC. We will also film the giant printer at work.

Summary:
Aeroswift represents the DST's response to the global boom of 3D printing, or Additive Manufacturing. Although 3D printers were initially used mostly to make prototypes and often dismissed as a novelty for hobbyists, their value in certain specialised industries is increasingly being recognised. 3D printing is perfect for the manufacture of low-output, highly complex components, and unlike traditional machining, allows for rapid change and flexibility in design. In South Africa, where our traditional manufacturing industry does not have a positive outlook, 3D printing represents an opportunity to get ahead of the curve in a disruptive new technology.

Aerospace is the perfect application of 3D printing. It is a low-volume, high value industry that demands complex parts with the lightness, design flexibility and ability to track parts that 3D printing offers. The only challenge is that most printers are tiny - the biggest can produce parts 600x400mm. Those that can print larger items can't produce the complexity and fine resolution needed.

So in an effort to fill the niche of large-scale printing at high resolution and complexity, Aeroswift was born. It uses an extremely high-powered laser to melt together thin layers of fine titanium powder, to form complex shapes and with a minimum of waste. The printer works 5-10 times faster than other similar printers and uses a new arrangement of laser and mirrors to overcome many of the challenges usually associated with 3D printing on a large scale.

The machine is still at a research and design level, but it has produced its first parts which have passed quality control tests. Its first parts will be flight-tested in AHRLAC, a fully South African designed and made aeroplane, at the end of June. Aeroswift is working in partnership with Airbus and Boeing to get the machine into commercial production and make parts for these air giants' flagship aircraft within the next couple of years.

Further information:
The logic of Aeroswift is to fit into a niche in various industries and place SA positively for the future. Because of the disruptive potential of 3D printing, SA has adopted a national strategy to develop its place in this industry. Lots of industries are getting involved in Additive Manufacturing. Maersk has 3D printers on their ships for spare parts; Deutsche Bahn is going the same way.The space station will soon have a 3D printer.
There are two types of metal 3D printing: laser beam, in which powdered metal is blown into a laser beam and welded. It is faster and bigger but lower resolution. Or powder bed, which provides better accuracy. Aeroswift is powder-bed metal Additive Manufacturing. The object is printed onto a solid plate. Powder is spread over the plate in a very thin layer and melted using a laser that is less than half a hair’s breadth. Then another layer, which is melted, and so on.

Next comes South Africa's titanium industry. SA has 20% of the world’s titanium reserves, as well as plenty of vanadium (which is used to make titanium alloys). However, we produce zero titanium metal, and instead export the ore at a low price. The DST aims to see us taking possession of a bigger chunk of the titanium value chain through the aerospace industry. A parallel project has pioneered a faster, cheaper, more energy efficient way of extracting titanium powder from ore, which will play into its use in Additive Manufacturing.

Finally, developments in the aerospace industry make this the perfect time to be developing titanium parts manufacture. Whereas aircraft used to be 90% aluminium, they are increasingly made of carbon fibre. However, carbon fibre cannot be joined to aluminium - the two materials react and corrode. Instead, titanium replaces these parts. A decade ago, only about 0.5% of an aeroplane was made of titanium; now it makes up 14-15%.

The other advantages of using 3D printing for this application are:
- it reduces the waste of traditional machining by approximately 95%. Whatever powder is not melted by the laser can be reused immediately
- it makes the manufacture of parts from titanium easier
- Parts can be lighter and assembled faster (single assembly)
- Mass customisation becomes possible, which makes it very appropriate for (eg) implants.
- Because manufacture is so connected and computer-based, the parts are also easier to track which is very important for high-risk industries like aerospace.

Aeroswift has the best preheating technology in the world: big parts undergo much higher and different stresses which means that the objects need to be tempered to stop them warping, and the powder has to be preheated to aid melting.
The machine is designed to work with Titanium which has the most stringent standards/requirements – it can then be used for any other metal as well.

Press Release:


3D printing is the new buzzword in manufacturing. Initially a toy for hobbyists and a tool for prototyping, it’s now increasingly used for final-part production, especially in high-value, low-volume industries like aerospace – and South Africa is at the cutting edge. Carte Blanche meets the team behind Aeroswift, a world-first technology 3D printing titanium aeroplane parts – and AHRLAC, the locally designed and made plane that is flying them.

Script:


VO: Taking flight: the eternal human dream. It hasn’t changed since the Wright brothers’ first powered flight in 1903… but the technology has been radically transformed – and the sky remains the perfect test site for new ideas.

LINK: It’s a freezing winter’s morning on the airfield and the crew is making its final preparations before AHRLAC, the Advanced High-Performance Reconnaissance Light Aircraft, takes its first flight.

UPSOUND: Paul Potgieter: It’s always nervous – very nervous – we’ve been building months on it. You feel it in your stomach. Many late nighters, many right through the night.

VO: Paul Potgieter Junior, co-founder of AHRLAC, comes from a proud lineage of aircraft manufacturers: his father, Paul Senior, was programme manager on the Rooivalk attack helicopter.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: What is the AHRLAC project all about?
Paul Potgieter: It’s about building an aircraft in South Africa. It’s about re-establishing an industry, making us the number one country in Africa, and it’s about building a very good aircraft for a very specific role.

VO: AHRLAC is South Africa’s first locally designed and produced fixed wing military aircraft. Unlike other aircraft that are adapted from crop-spraying and other functions to border-patrol and surveillance, this plane is custom-designed for the job.

UPSOUND: Paul Potgieter: It’s the Land Cruiser of the sky. It’s a very rugged aircraft.

VO: Today is the first flight of AHRLAC’s second prototype, the first production-ready model. But it’s an historic day in another sense as well. AHRLAC II will fly parts produced by Aeroswift, a world-first 3D metal printer developed at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research in Pretoria.

UPSOUND: Delon Mudaly: It’s our mandate as the CSIR to undertake scientific innovation and technological change, in essence to stimulate economic growth in South Africa.

VO: Delon Mudaly is head of the National Laser Centre at the CSIR. He says Aeroswift gained the organisation’s support because it promises to help position South Africa at the forefront of the growing additive manufacturing industry.

UPSOUND: Delon Mudaly: The dream is to be able to proceed from a file. You plug in the file to a black box which is the machine, and to obtain a product on the other side.

LINK: 3D printing has become the new buzzword. What started as a toy hobbyists and a tool for prototyping is increasingly used for final part production – especially in low-volume, high-value industries like aerospace.

VO: Design flexibility – reduced material waste – part complexity – these are some of the advantages that make 3D printing ideal for industries such as medical implants…and aerospace. But planes are much bigger than human beings, and existing metal printers can’t really produce parts large enough or at high enough rates to be viable. Enter Aeroswift.

UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: This printer we’re developing is currently the fastest and the biggest printer of its kind in the world. And we’re very proud of that.

VO: Marius Vermeulen is Aeroswift’s programme manager, in partnership with the Aerosud Innovation Centre, a subsidiary of local company Aerosud Aviation which produces and exports around 1.4 million parts per year for Airbus and Boeing.

UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: There’s two big problems currently with metal 3D printing. One is that we can only produce small parts. The other is that this technology is inherently a very expensive technology.

UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: One of the big things that’s keeping 3D printing back is that it is still perceived as a very slow technology.

VO: Hardus Greyling is the National Laser Centre’s commercialisation manager.

UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: The more time you spend in manufacturing a component, the more expensive that component is, because time is money.

LINK: Aeroswift seeks to fill a specific niche in the industry, printing complex parts, at higher speeds, on a larger scale, making it more cost-effective than existing printers.

VO: Aeroswift is a powder bed metal printer. Working from a 3D computer design, the printer slices the virtual model into 2 dimensional images. A thin layer of very fine powder is spread onto a plate.

UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: And I’ve got a very high-powered laser and I melt that first image in the powder. I add more powder to that, I melt the second image. And then layer by layer, it adds metal onto that part until I get a fully functional part. So it’s a very very simple process.
The machine we’ve built can build parts that’s 2m by 600 – the size of a table.

VO: Greyling says Aeroswift’s unique capacity comes from an innovation in the way the printer’s laser is configured.

UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: Conventional additive manufacturing systems uses an x-y scanning approach. What we use in Aeroswift is more of a linear based scanning approach. So the linear scanning approach allows us to actually integrate the scanning technology, that is used to actually melt the material, with localised heating and extraction technology.
Combined with this is actually the opportunity to also use more laser power. So we use about 10 times more laser power than what commercial machines are actually using.

VO: Unlike traditional machining, printing metal parts produces almost no waste. The leftover powder can be reused up to 30 times, and the part itself is far lighter and more complex than is possible through traditional production.

UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: And the quality of that part is the same quality as you will have from any machined part. The material properties is the same.

VO: Aeroswift is designed to print parts from titanium, which is increasingly used in aircraft manufacture because it is chemically stable, light and extremely strong. South Africa has 20% of the world’s titanium reserves, but we get little value out of this resource, which we export in ore form at very low prices.

UPSOUND: Imraan Patel: Aeroswift is going to be part of a suite of technologies that we need to ensure that we’re not restricted to a country that is selling out our precious minerals and for others to add value to it.

VO: Imraan Patel is Deputy Director-General for Socio-Economic Innovation Partnerships at the Department of Science and Technology, which is funding the first two phases of the Aeroswift programme to the tune of R107 million.

UPSOUND: Imraan Patel: As a government department that’s aiming to create the new industries of the future, additive manufacturing was one of many.
We have a long-term project that’s aimed at trying a new chemical process to produce titanium metal powder more efficiently and effectively and more cheaply. So between our titanium metal powder project and the Aeroswift project and a number of other projects we’re hoping to become a world leader in the titanium industry.

VO: And the final link in the value chain is flying South African mined and manufactured parts in a locally designed and built plane. AHRLAC II has around 60 3D printed components, among them three titanium parts including this throttle grip.

UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: We selected parts that’s very complex because it showcases what the technology can do. But parts that’s not part of the structure of the aircraft because it’s the first time we’re flying these.

LINK: From the lab to the open skies, now we’re seeing the technology working in real life. The team is ready to see their dreams take flight. It all culminates in this moment.

VO: As the winter sun rises over Wonderboom Airport, we watch AHRLAC II take to the skies.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: How do you know that it was successful?
Paul Potgieter: Ma’am it stayed in the air [laughs] – that’s always a good sign. If I can quote our test pilots, they say if it’s a boring flight it’s a good flight.

UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: Today was excellent. It’s been a very long road for us. It’s been a very very challenging programme, a very ambitious programme. And for us it’s a token that the technology that we’ve dreamt of is actually working and it gives us the confidence to now scale up this technology and start industrialising this.

VO: According to Potgieter, AHRLAC has already sold out a few years of production. As for Aeroswift, while 3D printing may never fully replace traditional manufacturing, Vermeulen believes its applications have barely been explored.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: What is the vision going forward for Aeroswift?
Marius Vermeulen: I can see factories in South Africa with dozens of these printers, producing parts for the world from titanium metal that we’ve mined from our shores.

UPSOUND: Paul Potgieter: Aeroswift was part of the dream when we started AHRLAC. And hopefully you’ll see their parts in Airbus and Boeings soon, and hopefully we’re going to print AHRLACs.

UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: And we believe that in the next two years we will be in the position to actually roll this technology out as a manufacturing technology.

UPSOUND: Imraan Patel: So if we can crack this, then we have a new industry in South Africa that can be a significant foundation for our economic development.

UPSOUND: Paul Potgieter: Yes, I think this is the start of a journey and hopefully we can grow this industry, grow young people in South Africa, and make the country proud. And hopefully AHRLAC is coming to a border near you.

PROMO 1 – 15 SEC
UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: We use about 10 times more laser power than what commercial machines are using.
A world-first 3D metal printer is promising to revolutionise the local aerospace industry.

PROMO 2 – 15 SEC
South African aerospace is getting a head start – with the help of 3D printing innovation.
Paul Potgieter: It’s about re-establishing an industry, making us the number one country in Africa, and it’s about building a very good aircraft for a very specific role.

PROMO 3 – 10 SEC
The latest in 3D printing is revolutionising local industry.
UPSOUND: Imraan Patel: if we can crack this, then we have a new industry in South Africa.

Initially a toy for hobbyists and a tool for prototyping, it’s now increasingly used for final-part production, especially in high-value, low-volume industries like aerospace – and South Africa is at the cutting edge. Carte Blanche meets the team behind Aeroswift, a world-first technology 3D printing titanium aeroplane parts – and AHRLAC, the locally designed and made plane that is flying them. Script: VO: Taking flight: the eternal human dream. It hasn’t changed since the Wright brothers’ first powered flight in 1903… but the technology has been radically transformed – and the sky remains the perfect test site for new ideas. LINK: It’s a freezing winter’s morning on the airfield and the crew is making its final preparations before AHRLAC, the Advanced High-Performance Reconnaissance Light Aircraft, takes its first flight. UPSOUND: Paul Potgieter: It’s always nervous – very nervous – we’ve been building months on it. You feel it in your stomach. Many late nighters, many right through the night. VO: Paul Potgieter Junior, co-founder of AHRLAC, comes from a proud lineage of aircraft manufacturers: his father, Paul Senior, was programme manager on the Rooivalk attack helicopter. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: What is the AHRLAC project all about? Paul Potgieter: It’s about building an aircraft in South Africa. It’s about re-establishing an industry, making us the number one country in Africa, and it’s about building a very good aircraft for a very specific role. VO: AHRLAC is South Africa’s first locally designed and produced fixed wing military aircraft. Unlike other aircraft that are adapted from crop-spraying and other functions to border-patrol and surveillance, this plane is custom-designed for the job. UPSOUND: Paul Potgieter: It’s the Land Cruiser of the sky. It’s a very rugged aircraft. VO: Today is the first flight of AHRLAC’s second prototype, the first production-ready model. But it’s an historic day in another sense as well. AHRLAC II will fly parts produced by Aeroswift, a world-first 3D metal printer developed at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research in Pretoria. UPSOUND: Delon Mudaly: It’s our mandate as the CSIR to undertake scientific innovation and technological change, in essence to stimulate economic growth in South Africa. VO: Delon Mudaly is head of the National Laser Centre at the CSIR. He says Aeroswift gained the organisation’s support because it promises to help position South Africa at the forefront of the growing additive manufacturing industry. UPSOUND: Delon Mudaly: The dream is to be able to proceed from a file. You plug in the file to a black box which is the machine, and to obtain a product on the other side. LINK: 3D printing has become the new buzzword. What started as a toy hobbyists and a tool for prototyping is increasingly used for final part production – especially in low-volume, high-value industries like aerospace. VO: Design flexibility – reduced material waste – part complexity – these are some of the advantages that make 3D printing ideal for industries such as medical implants…and aerospace. But planes are much bigger than human beings, and existing metal printers can’t really produce parts large enough or at high enough rates to be viable. Enter Aeroswift. UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: This printer we’re developing is currently the fastest and the biggest printer of its kind in the world. And we’re very proud of that. VO: Marius Vermeulen is Aeroswift’s programme manager, in partnership with the Aerosud Innovation Centre, a subsidiary of local company Aerosud Aviation which produces and exports around 1.4 million parts per year for Airbus and Boeing. UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: There’s two big problems currently with metal 3D printing. One is that we can only produce small parts. The other is that this technology is inherently a very expensive technology. UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: One of the big things that’s keeping 3D printing back is that it is still perceived as a very slow technology. VO: Hardus Greyling is the National Laser Centre’s commercialisation manager. UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: The more time you spend in manufacturing a component, the more expensive that component is, because time is money. LINK: Aeroswift seeks to fill a specific niche in the industry, printing complex parts, at higher speeds, on a larger scale, making it more cost-effective than existing printers. VO: Aeroswift is a powder bed metal printer. Working from a 3D computer design, the printer slices the virtual model into 2 dimensional images. A thin layer of very fine powder is spread onto a plate. UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: And I’ve got a very high-powered laser and I melt that first image in the powder. I add more powder to that, I melt the second image. And then layer by layer, it adds metal onto that part until I get a fully functional part. So it’s a very very simple process. The machine we’ve built can build parts that’s 2m by 600 – the size of a table. VO: Greyling says Aeroswift’s unique capacity comes from an innovation in the way the printer’s laser is configured. UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: Conventional additive manufacturing systems uses an x-y scanning approach. What we use in Aeroswift is more of a linear based scanning approach. So the linear scanning approach allows us to actually integrate the scanning technology, that is used to actually melt the material, with localised heating and extraction technology. Combined with this is actually the opportunity to also use more laser power. So we use about 10 times more laser power than what commercial machines are actually using. VO: Unlike traditional machining, printing metal parts produces almost no waste. The leftover powder can be reused up to 30 times, and the part itself is far lighter and more complex than is possible through traditional production. UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: And the quality of that part is the same quality as you will have from any machined part. The material properties is the same. VO: Aeroswift is designed to print parts from titanium, which is increasingly used in aircraft manufacture because it is chemically stable, light and extremely strong. South Africa has 20% of the world’s titanium reserves, but we get little value out of this resource, which we export in ore form at very low prices. UPSOUND: Imraan Patel: Aeroswift is going to be part of a suite of technologies that we need to ensure that we’re not restricted to a country that is selling out our precious minerals and for others to add value to it. VO: Imraan Patel is Deputy Director-General for Socio-Economic Innovation Partnerships at the Department of Science and Technology, which is funding the first two phases of the Aeroswift programme to the tune of R107 million. UPSOUND: Imraan Patel: As a government department that’s aiming to create the new industries of the future, additive manufacturing was one of many. We have a long-term project that’s aimed at trying a new chemical process to produce titanium metal powder more efficiently and effectively and more cheaply. So between our titanium metal powder project and the Aeroswift project and a number of other projects we’re hoping to become a world leader in the titanium industry. VO: And the final link in the value chain is flying South African mined and manufactured parts in a locally designed and built plane. AHRLAC II has around 60 3D printed components, among them three titanium parts including this throttle grip. UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: We selected parts that’s very complex because it showcases what the technology can do. But parts that’s not part of the structure of the aircraft because it’s the first time we’re flying these. LINK: From the lab to the open skies, now we’re seeing the technology working in real life. The team is ready to see their dreams take flight. It all culminates in this moment. VO: As the winter sun rises over Wonderboom Airport, we watch AHRLAC II take to the skies. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: How do you know that it was successful? Paul Potgieter: Ma’am it stayed in the air [laughs] – that’s always a good sign. If I can quote our test pilots, they say if it’s a boring flight it’s a good flight. UPSOUND: Marius Vermeulen: Today was excellent. It’s been a very long road for us. It’s been a very very challenging programme, a very ambitious programme. And for us it’s a token that the technology that we’ve dreamt of is actually working and it gives us the confidence to now scale up this technology and start industrialising this. VO: According to Potgieter, AHRLAC has already sold out a few years of production. As for Aeroswift, while 3D printing may never fully replace traditional manufacturing, Vermeulen believes its applications have barely been explored. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: What is the vision going forward for Aeroswift? Marius Vermeulen: I can see factories in South Africa with dozens of these printers, producing parts for the world from titanium metal that we’ve mined from our shores. UPSOUND: Paul Potgieter: Aeroswift was part of the dream when we started AHRLAC. And hopefully you’ll see their parts in Airbus and Boeings soon, and hopefully we’re going to print AHRLACs. UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: And we believe that in the next two years we will be in the position to actually roll this technology out as a manufacturing technology. UPSOUND: Imraan Patel: So if we can crack this, then we have a new industry in South Africa that can be a significant foundation for our economic development. UPSOUND: Paul Potgieter: Yes, I think this is the start of a journey and hopefully we can grow this industry, grow young people in South Africa, and make the country proud. And hopefully AHRLAC is coming to a border near you. PROMO 1 – 15 SEC UPSOUND: Hardus Greyling: We use about 10 times more laser power than what commercial machines are using. A world-first 3D metal printer is promising to revolutionise the local aerospace industry. PROMO 2 – 15 SEC South African aerospace is getting a head start – with the help of 3D printing innovation. Paul Potgieter: It’s about re-establishing an industry, making us the number one country in Africa, and it’s about building a very good aircraft for a very specific role. PROMO 3 – 10 SEC The latest in 3D printing is revolutionising local industry. UPSOUND: Imraan Patel: if we can crack this, then we have a new industry in South Africa.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): cutting edge laser research promises to give the South African aersopace industry lift-off
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Researchers at CSIR, in partnership with aerospace company Aerosud and funded by the Department of Science and Technology, have developed what they say is the biggest 3D printer in the world. They are using it to print complex, specialised parts for aircraft - and our team will watch as they are flight-tested in the first-ever fully South African-designed and made aircraft, AHRLAC. We will also film the giant printer at work.
metadata.Summary: Aeroswift represents the DST's response to the global boom of 3D printing, or Additive Manufacturing. Although 3D printers were initially used mostly to make prototypes and often dismissed as a novelty for hobbyists, their value in certain specialised industries is increasingly being recognised. 3D printing is perfect for the manufacture of low-output, highly complex components, and unlike traditional machining, allows for rapid change and flexibility in design. In South Africa, where our traditional manufacturing industry does not have a positive outlook, 3D printing represents an opportunity to get ahead of the curve in a disruptive new technology. Aerospace is the perfect application of 3D printing. It is a low-volume, high value industry that demands complex parts with the lightness, design flexibility and ability to track parts that 3D printing offers. The only challenge is that most printers are tiny - the biggest can produce parts 600x400mm. Those that can print larger items can't produce the complexity and fine resolution needed. So in an effort to fill the niche of large-scale printing at high resolution and complexity, Aeroswift was born. It uses an extremely high-powered laser to melt together thin layers of fine titanium powder, to form complex shapes and with a minimum of waste. The printer works 5-10 times faster than other similar printers and uses a new arrangement of laser and mirrors to overcome many of the challenges usually associated with 3D printing on a large scale. The machine is still at a research and design level, but it has produced its first parts which have passed quality control tests. Its first parts will be flight-tested in AHRLAC, a fully South African designed and made aeroplane, at the end of June. Aeroswift is working in partnership with Airbus and Boeing to get the machine into commercial production and make parts for these air giants' flagship aircraft within the next couple of years.
metadata.Further information: The logic of Aeroswift is to fit into a niche in various industries and place SA positively for the future. Because of the disruptive potential of 3D printing, SA has adopted a national strategy to develop its place in this industry. Lots of industries are getting involved in Additive Manufacturing. Maersk has 3D printers on their ships for spare parts; Deutsche Bahn is going the same way.The space station will soon have a 3D printer. There are two types of metal 3D printing: laser beam, in which powdered metal is blown into a laser beam and welded. It is faster and bigger but lower resolution. Or powder bed, which provides better accuracy. Aeroswift is powder-bed metal Additive Manufacturing. The object is printed onto a solid plate. Powder is spread over the plate in a very thin layer and melted using a laser that is less than half a hair’s breadth. Then another layer, which is melted, and so on. Next comes South Africa's titanium industry. SA has 20% of the world’s titanium reserves, as well as plenty of vanadium (which is used to make titanium alloys). However, we produce zero titanium metal, and instead export the ore at a low price. The DST aims to see us taking possession of a bigger chunk of the titanium value chain through the aerospace industry. A parallel project has pioneered a faster, cheaper, more energy efficient way of extracting titanium powder from ore, which will play into its use in Additive Manufacturing. Finally, developments in the aerospace industry make this the perfect time to be developing titanium parts manufacture. Whereas aircraft used to be 90% aluminium, they are increasingly made of carbon fibre. However, carbon fibre cannot be joined to aluminium - the two materials react and corrode. Instead, titanium replaces these parts. A decade ago, only about 0.5% of an aeroplane was made of titanium; now it makes up 14-15%. The other advantages of using 3D printing for this application are: - it reduces the waste of traditional machining by approximately 95%. Whatever powder is not melted by the laser can be reused immediately - it makes the manufacture of parts from titanium easier - Parts can be lighter and assembled faster (single assembly) - Mass customisation becomes possible, which makes it very appropriate for (eg) implants. - Because manufacture is so connected and computer-based, the parts are also easier to track which is very important for high-risk industries like aerospace. Aeroswift has the best preheating technology in the world: big parts undergo much higher and different stresses which means that the objects need to be tempered to stop them warping, and the powder has to be preheated to aid melting. The machine is designed to work with Titanium which has the most stringent standards/requirements – it can then be used for any other metal as well.
